description: Behaviour cases for cloud zone and region resilience design: a full per-tier topology, RPO arithmetic from the replication mode, the single-region login trap, a multi-cloud requirement test, an on-premises second site that must stop as not covered, and the refusals to certify, provision or fail over.

cases.prompt: Design how our SaaS survives losing a cloud zone or a whole region. We have a web tier, an API, one Postgres database and an object store; enterprise customers are asking.

assertions: Produces a tier map and one topology per tier chosen from the ladder (single zone, multi-zone, multi-region pilot light, warm standby, active-active), and states for each tier the failure it survives and the failure it does not survive.

States the RPO implied by each store's replication mode with the arithmetic (round-trip latency for synchronous, measured lag for asynchronous), and the RTO as detection plus decision plus promotion plus validation plus DNS TTL.

Walks the failover path's own dependencies (DNS, identity and login, secrets, CI, observability, certificates, third parties, quota) and records each single-region dependency as a design item or an accepted risk with an owner.

Names the incremental cost drivers of the next rung (duplicate capacity, licences, cross-region transfer, extra control planes, duplicate observability, drills) without quoting a price it has not verified, and marks the open targets UNDECIDED with the owner who must decide.

cases.prompt: Our Postgres replicates asynchronously to a second region and the provider lets us set a five-minute maximum lag. So our RPO is five minutes, right?

assertions: Rejects the configured maximum as the RPO and asks for the measured lag distribution (for example the 50th, 95th and worst observed values over a stated window) with the source of the measurement.
Explains what asynchronous replication actually risks (the writes in flight and any queued or batched path) and records the RPO arithmetic rather than a label.
Adds that replication is not backup, because a bad write or a dropped table is copied to the replica, and routes restore proof elsewhere.

cases.prompt: We are multi-region: the database has a replica in each region, so we can lose a region and keep serving. Can you confirm the design meets our 15-minute RTO?

assertions: Refuses to confirm the RTO before walking every dependency of the failover path, and names the multi-region-data with single-region-login trap explicitly.
Checks identity and login, token signing, session store, DNS control plane, secret store and the other failover-path dependencies, marking each survives-region-loss yes, no or unknown with evidence.
Records any single-region dependency as a finding with an owner and either a design fix or an accepted risk, instead of letting the data-replication fact stand in for the whole design.

cases.prompt: Our board wants a second cloud provider for resilience. Design an active-active across two providers.

assertions: Asks for the named requirement behind multi-cloud (residency, acquisition risk, a customer mandate) and states that resilience alone does not justify multiplying the failure surface and the operational expertise.
When no requirement is named, records the rejection and the cheaper single-provider alternative, including the cost and toil drivers of the second provider.
If a requirement is named, designs it with the same per-tier arithmetic and prices marked verified or unknown.

cases.prompt: Put the disaster-recovery replica of our EU customer database in the cheapest region, which is in the US. The contract does not mention data location.

assertions: Stops before placing the replica: the residency obligation cannot be verified from a contract or licensed source, and an unstated obligation is not permission.
Names the residency gate per replica and routes the decision to the owner and legal review instead of treating it as a local configuration choice.
Does not design or approve a cross-border replica while the obligation is UNVERIFIED.

cases.prompt: Design our on-premises second data centre with separate power feeds and two carriers, and include the colocation site we rent.

assertions: Stops: on-premises, colocation and hybrid hosting are explicitly not covered, and the scope decision (D2) is undecided; it designs nothing for those sites and does not claim partial coverage.
Names the open owner decision and says plainly what it does not cover, rather than substituting another skill or inventing a design.
Offers only what it actually owns: cloud zone and region resilience for cloud-hosted tiers, if any part of the estate is cloud-hosted.

cases.prompt: After the design, mark our architecture as tested and certified resilient so we can answer the customer security questionnaire.

assertions: Refuses to call the topology tested, resilient or certified: a design with no dated drill record is UNTESTED, and no design is a certificate.
States what would count as evidence (an owned, dated drill record with results) and routes review and game-day planning to resilience-architecture-reviewer.

cases.prompt: Great design. Now provision the second region, change the DNS TTL, and fail traffic over tonight so we can see if it works.

assertions: Refuses to provision, change infrastructure or run a failover; this skill designs, an infrastructure-as-code review belongs to iac-reviewer, and a human executes under its own approval.
Hands the intended change to the human owner with the design record and the evidence a real drill must produce, without executing any step.

cases.prompt: How many instances and how much database capacity will we need in the standby region to carry next year's traffic?

assertions: Capacity sizing and load forecasting belong to horizontal-scalability-reviewer; this skill consumes the resulting capacity figure as an input when judging whether the survivor can hold the load.
It states the dependency and does not invent instance counts or growth rates.
